   ONCOR ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION
                      SERVICES CORPORATION’S
    OBJECTIONS TO, AND MOTION TO STRIKE, INTERVENOR TESTIMONY

       Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA TSC,” together, “Applicants”) hereby file these objections to intervenor

testimony and respectfully move to strike. Pursuant to State Office of Administrative Hearings

(“SOAH”) Order No. 6, these objections are timely filed.

                                   I.     INTRODUCTION

       Well over 700 pieces of testimony consisting of thousands of pages were filed in this

proceeding on and prior to May 13, 2026. Applicants have endeavored to review and assess the

admissibility of such testimony in an expedited time frame in accordance with the requirements of

SOAH Order No. 6. While Applicants support the ability of landowners to assert and provide the

Public Utility Commission of Texas (the “Commission”) with their views and concerns regarding

the proposed Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765 kV transmission line project (the

“Project”), some of the testimony and testimony attachments presented are not reasonably

admissible in this proceeding as filed. A comprehensive list of testimony and attachments to which


APPLICANTS’ OBJECTIONS AND MOTION TO STRIKE INTERVENOR TESTIMONY                          - PAGE 1
 Applicants are objecting and moving to strike, along with the corresponding bases for objecting

and moving to strike, is attached hereto as Exhibit A and incorporated herein by reference. A

discussion of arguments supporting each objection is contained below.

                                      II.      NON-EXPERT OPINION

           Many parties’ pre-filed testimony in this proceeding express opinions, views, concerns, or

comments on scientific, technical, legal, or other specialized matters. Under Texas Rule of

Evidence 702, expert testimony is admissible only when the proponent shows that the (1)

“scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will assist the trier of fact,” and (2) the

testifying witness qualifies as an expert based on “knowledge, skill, experience, training, or

education.” 1 To the extent that pre-filed testimony includes expert testimony from an unqualified

witness, Applicants object and move to strike the offending portions.

           The party offering the expert’s testimony bears the burden to prove that the witness is

qualified under Rule 702. 2 Moreover, the offering party must demonstrate that the witness

“possesses special knowledge as to the very matter on which he proposes to give an opinion.”3

Several witnesses for which pre-filed testimony was presented in this proceeding included

evidence supporting their qualification to proffer testimony in accordance with Texas Rule of

Evidence 702. Many did not. Applicants acknowledge that many landowners have substantial

background and experience regarding their properties, often spanning years or generations of

ownership, or regarding the cattle and wildlife that inhabit their land. However, such familiarity

falls short of the standard under the Texas Rules of Evidence for offering expert opinions regarding



1
    Tex. R. Evid. 702.

2
    Gammill v. Jack Williams Chevrolet, 972 S.W.2d 713, 718 (Tex. 1998) (internal citation omitted).

3
    Id.


APPLICANTS’ OBJECTIONS AND MOTION TO STRIKE INTERVENOR TESTIMONY                                       - PAGE 2
 technical or scientific matters. 4 Experience and familiarity with land and wildlife is insufficient to

establish qualification as an expert to testify to, for example, a transmission line’s purported impact

to the land and wildlife.

           Applicants’ Exhibit A includes a list of testimony excerpts and attachments that constitute

impermissible expert testimony by an unqualified witness. Generally, the witnesses are providing

opinions concerning technical matters such as the potential health effects of electric and magnetic

fields, wildlife biology, ecology, hydrology, property valuation and appraisals, electric

engineering, power flow dynamics, or legal requirements. For the reasons stated herein, such

testimony is objectionable and should be struck.

                                             III.     RELEVANCE

           The Order of Referral and Preliminary Order in this proceeding identifies as an issue not

to be addressed:

           1.       What is the appropriate compensation for right-of-way or condemnation of

                    property?

           Many of the pre-filed testimonies in this proceeding include statements, conclusions, or

assertions regarding the valuation impact of the Project on a particular property. Evidence

regarding the potential adverse economic effects on, or diminution in the present or future value

of, an intervenor’s property resulting from the proposed line is not relevant to this proceeding. 5

Indeed, the Commission’s order has expressly precluded consideration of property valuation

impacts and compensable loss, reserving such issues for resolution in eminent domain

proceedings.


4
    See generally, E.I. du Pont de Nemours and Co., Inc. v. Robinson, 923 S.W.2d 549, 554 (Tex. 1995).

5
    See Tex. R. Evid. 401, 402.



APPLICANTS’ OBJECTIONS AND MOTION TO STRIKE INTERVENOR TESTIMONY                                         - PAGE 3
            Pursuant to the preliminary order in this proceeding, Applicants respectfully object to the

admission of statements regarding the value of a particular property and the potential right-of-way

cost or financial damage, as outlined in Exhibit A, and move to strike the offending portions from

pre-filed testimony.

                                                IV.       HEARSAY

           Hearsay is not admissible except as provided by rule or statute. 6 Evidence is hearsay when

its probative value depends in whole or in part on competency or credibility of some person other

than the person by whom it is sought to be produced. 7

           Statements and exhibits attached to direct testimony that rely on or incorporate the

statements or opinions of third parties constitute inadmissible hearsay. Such evidence has little to

no probative value in establishing impacts on property values (which, as discussed above, is not at

issue in this proceeding), potential health effects, or other matters. This is particularly true where

the proffered evidence consists of newspaper articles, magazine pieces, websites, or blog posts,

the reliability of which depends entirely on the credibility of individuals who are not witnesses in

this case.

           Because such materials reflect the views of individuals who are not parties to this

proceeding, have not submitted testimony or statements of position, and cannot be cross‑examined,

these out‑of‑court statements are hearsay and therefore inadmissible.




6
    Tex. R. Evid. 802. Texas Rule of Evidence 801 defines hearsay as a statement, other than one made by the

declarant while testifying, offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted.

7
    Chandler v. Chandler, 842 S.W.2d 829, 831 (Tex. App.—El Paso 1992, writ denied); Texarkana

Mack Sales, Inc. v. Flemister, 741 S.W.2d 558, 562 (Tex. App.—Texarkana 1987, no writ).



APPLICANTS’ OBJECTIONS AND MOTION TO STRIKE INTERVENOR TESTIMONY                                               - PAGE 4
        The testimony and exhibits listed in Exhibit A do not fall within any hearsay exceptions

set forth in the Texas Rules of Evidence. Respectfully, it is inappropriate for testimony in this

proceeding to introduce and rely on statements purporting to represent the position of non-parties

regarding the potential impacts of the Project or for those statements to be admitted into evidence

and cited for their truth. Accordingly, Applicants request Your Honors strike the testimony and

attachments identified in Exhibit A from pre-filed testimony.


                                     V.      CONCLUSION

       For the reasons presented above, Applicants respectfully object to the admission of the

testimony and exhibits identified in Exhibit A for the reasons stated herein.

the reliability of which depends entirely on the credibility of individuals who are not witnesses in
